facts.claim: H.Con.Res. 86's order to remove U.S. forces from any hostilities against Iran excludes forces that may be needed to defend the United States or an ally or partner from imminent attack. facts.quote: other than those elements of the Armed Forces that may be necessary to defend the United States or an ally or partner of the United States from imminent attack provided that the President complies fully with the requirements of section 5(b) the War Powers Resolution (50 U.S.C. 1544(b)) with respect to any such use of the Armed Forces

facts.claim: The War Powers Resolution, a federal law, says that when U.S. forces are fighting outside U.S. territory without a declaration of war or a law specifically authorizing it, the President must remove them if Congress so directs by a concurrent resolution, a measure passed by the House and Senate.
facts.quote: at any time that United States Armed Forces are engaged in hostilities outside the territory of the United States, its possessions and territories without a declaration of war or specific statutory authorization, such forces shall be removed by the President if the Congress so directs by concurrent resolution

facts.claim: If H.Con.Res. 86 fails, the War Powers Resolution's 60-day limit applies: the President must end any use of U.S. forces in fighting within 60 days after the report to Congress on it is sent or due, whichever is first, unless Congress declares war, authorizes it by law or extends the limit by law.
facts.quote: Within sixty calendar days after a report is submitted or is required to be submitted pursuant to section 1543(a)(1) of this title, whichever is earlier, the President shall terminate any use of United States Armed Forces with respect to which such report was submitted (or required to be submitted), unless the Congress (1) has declared war or has enacted a specific authorization for such use of United States Armed Forces, (2) has extended by law such sixty-day period

facts.claim: The War Powers Resolution, a federal law, says the President's power as commander in chief to send U.S. forces into fighting is used only after a declaration of war, under a law specifically allowing it, or in an emergency created by an attack on the United States, its territories or its forces.
facts.quote: The constitutional powers of the President as Commander-in-Chief to introduce United States Armed Forces into hostilities, or into situations where imminent involvement in hostilities is clearly indicated by the circumstances, are exercised only pursuant to (1) a declaration of war, (2) specific statutory authorization, or (3) a national emergency created by attack upon the United States, its territories or possessions, or its armed forces.

facts.claim: The War Powers Resolution's 60-day limit on using U.S. forces in fighting does not apply if an armed attack leaves Congress unable to meet. The limit is extended by up to 30 days if the President certifies in writing to Congress that the troops' safety requires the extra time to remove them.
facts.quote: (3) is physically unable to meet as a result of an armed attack upon the United States. Such sixty-day period shall be extended for not more than an additional thirty days if the President determines and certifies to the Congress in writing that unavoidable military necessity respecting the safety of United States Armed Forces requires the continued use of such armed forces in the course of bringing about a prompt removal of such forces.

facts.claim: The War Powers Resolution, a federal law, requires the President, within 48 hours of sending U.S. forces into fighting (or some other situations abroad) without a declaration of war, to send Congress's leaders a written report on why, under what legal authority, and for how long and how widely.
facts.quote: In the absence of a declaration of war, in any case in which United States Armed Forces are introduced— (1) into hostilities or into situations where imminent involvement in hostilities is clearly indicated by the circumstances; (2) into the territory, airspace or waters of a foreign nation, while equipped for combat, except for deployments which relate solely to supply, replacement, repair, or training of such forces; or (3) in numbers which substantially enlarge United States Armed Forces equipped for combat already located in a foreign nation; the President shall submit within 48 hours to the Speaker of the House of Representatives and to the President pro tempore of the Senate a report, in writing, setting forth— (A) the circumstances necessitating the introduction of United States Armed Forces; (B) the constitutional and legislative authority under which such introduction took place; and (C) the estimated scope and duration of the hostilities or involvement.

facts.claim: Congress overturns an Internal Revenue Service (IRS) rule published December 30, 2024. The rule loses all legal force. It required certain "decentralized finance" businesses, which help people trade digital assets like cryptocurrency, to report customers' sales to the IRS as brokers, from 2027 on.
facts.quote: Congress disapproves the rule submitted by the Internal Revenue Service relating to Gross Proceeds Reporting by Brokers That Regularly Provide Services Effectuating Digital Asset Sales (89 Fed. Reg. 106928 (December 30, 2024)), and such rule shall have no force or effect.

facts.claim: The Internal Revenue Service's (IRS's) December 30, 2024, broker rule required certain businesses in "decentralized finance" (DeFi) to file tax information forms with the IRS as brokers, and to give their customers statements.
facts.quote: to require certain decentralized finance industry participants to file and furnish information returns as brokers

facts.claim: The Internal Revenue Service's December 30, 2024, broker rule is about "decentralized finance" (DeFi). In DeFi, people trade digital assets through software that runs on its own ("smart contracts"), and no DeFi business holds the secret keys that control customers' assets.
facts.quote: The DeFi industry offers services that allow for transactions that use automatically executing software commonly referred to as smart contracts based on distributed ledger technology without any participant in the DeFi industry (DeFi participant) taking custody of the private keys used for accessing the digital asset customer's digital assets on a distributed ledger.

facts.claim: The Internal Revenue Service's (IRS's) December 30, 2024, rule treats only one kind of decentralized finance business as brokers: "trading front-end" services (the apps and websites people use to trade). The IRS said they are closest to customers and best placed to get their identifying information.
facts.quote: the only DeFi participants that should be treated as brokers are trading front-end service providers. This determination was made for several reasons, which are discussed in more detail in the remainder of this Part III. of this Summary of Comments and Explanation of Revisions. First, such providers are the DeFi participants that have the closest relationship to customers and therefore are in the best position to obtain customer identification information.

facts.claim: The "front-end" services that the Internal Revenue Service's December 30, 2024, rule treats as brokers are the screens, buttons and forms in websites, phone apps and browser add-ons that people use to trade digital assets kept in wallets they control themselves.
facts.quote: providing software (sometimes referred to as front-end services) that provides the digital asset user with tools--including screens, buttons, forms, and other visual elements incorporated in websites, mobile device apps, and browser extensions--that users can use to trade digital assets in their unhosted wallets

facts.claim: Under the Internal Revenue Service's broker rules, digital assets are any digital form of value that is not cash and is recorded on a secured shared database that records transactions across many computers (a "distributed ledger"), or similar technology.
facts.quote: digital assets, which are defined generally as any digital representation of value that is not cash and is recorded on a cryptographically secured distributed ledger (that is, a database that records transactions across multiple computers) or any similar technology

facts.claim: In the 2021 Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act, Congress extended brokers' tax reporting to digital assets. The Internal Revenue Service's December 30, 2024, rule says Congress did so to close or greatly reduce unpaid tax on unreported income and to give taxpayers information on their sales.
facts.quote: Congress extended the information reporting rules under section 6045 to digital assets to close or significantly reduce the income tax gap from unreported income and to provide information about these transactions to taxpayers. See 167 Cong. Rec. S5702, 5703 (daily ed. August 3, 2021) (Joint Committee on Taxation, Technical Explanation of Section 80603 of the Infrastructure Act).

facts.claim: If the resolution fails, the Internal Revenue Service's (IRS's) December 30, 2024, rule stays. Decentralized finance trading apps and websites treated as brokers must then report the money customers get from certain sales and trades of digital assets, both to the IRS and to the customers.
facts.quote: The final regulations require these brokers to file information returns and furnish payee statements reporting gross proceeds on dispositions of digital assets effected for customers in certain sale or exchange transactions.

facts.claim: If the resolution fails, decentralized finance brokers must report digital asset sales made on or after January 1, 2027, under the Internal Revenue Service's (IRS's) December 30, 2024, rule. The IRS set that later start because many might not yet have systems to collect and report the information.
facts.quote: the Treasury Department and the IRS agree that a delay is warranted for trading front-end service providers treated as brokers (DeFi brokers) under these final regulations. First, many of these DeFi brokers may not have systems in place to collect and store customer identity information or contracts with third-party service providers to do the same. Second, many of these DeFi brokers also may not have systems in place to collect, store, and report customer transaction information or contracts with third-party service providers to do the same. Third, many of these DeFi brokers also do not have backup withholding systems that would enable these brokers to backup withhold and pay the backup withholding tax in cash. Based on these considerations, final Sec. 1.6045-1(a)(21) applies to sales of digital assets occurring on or after January 1, 2027.

facts.claim: The Internal Revenue Service estimated that about 650 to 875 decentralized finance brokers would be affected by its December 30, 2024, rule, which required them to report customers' sales of digital assets to the agency.
facts.quote: the Treasury Department and the IRS have concluded that approximately 650 to 875 DeFi brokers, with a mid-point of approximately 765 DeFi brokers, will be impacted by these final regulations

facts.claim: The resolution does not overturn a July 2024 Internal Revenue Service rule on reporting by other digital asset brokers, such as trading platforms that hold their customers' assets.
facts.quote: On July 9, 2024, the Treasury Department and the IRS published in the Federal Register (89 FR 56480) final regulations (REG-122793-19) (TD 10000) regarding information reporting by certain brokers and the determination of amount realized and basis for certain digital asset sales and exchanges. TD 10000 generally applies to digital asset brokers that act as agents for a party in the transaction, such as operators of custodial digital asset trading platforms

facts.claim: Under the Congressional Review Act, the Internal Revenue Service may not issue its December 30, 2024, decentralized finance broker rule again, or one substantially the same, unless a law passed later specifically allows it.

facts.claim: Under the Clean Air Act, new vehicles face only two sets of pollution standards: the Environmental Protection Agency's, and California's, which California may enforce only with that agency's permission (called a "waiver"). Other states may adopt only standards identical to California's.
facts.quote: In sections 209(a) and 209(b) of the Clean Air Act, Congress established that there would be only two programs for control of emissions from new motor vehicles--EPA emission standards adopted under the Clean Air Act, and California emission standards adopted under state law. Congress accomplished this by preempting all State and local governments from adopting or attempting to enforce emission standards for new motor vehicles, while at the same time providing that California could receive a waiver of preemption for its emission standards and accompanying enforcement procedures. Other states can only adopt standards that are identical to California's standards.

facts.claim: The Environmental Protection Agency's April 6, 2023, decision let California enforce four of its heavy-duty vehicle rules: longer emissions warranties, Advanced Clean Trucks (zero-emission truck sales), zero-emission airport shuttles, and certifying zero-emission powertrains (motors, drive parts).
facts.quote: The Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) is granting the California Air Resources Board's (CARB's) requests for waivers of Clean Air Act (CAA) preemption for the following California regulations: the Heavy-Duty Vehicle and Engine Emission Warranty Regulations and Maintenance Provisions, the Advanced Clean Trucks Regulation, the Zero Emission Airport Shuttle Regulation, and the Zero-Emission Power Train Certification Regulation.

facts.claim: If the resolution fails, California keeps the Environmental Protection Agency's April 6, 2023, permission to enforce its Advanced Clean Trucks rule. It requires makers to sell a rising share of zero- and near-zero-emission medium- and heavy-duty vehicles in California, starting with 2024 models.
facts.quote: The ACT Regulation, adopted by the CARB Board on January 26, 2021, requires that manufacturers produce and sell increasing percentages of medium- and heavy-duty zero-emission vehicles (ZEVs) and near zero-emission vehicles (NZEVs) in California. These quantities of vehicles are based on increasingly higher percentages of manufacturers' annual sales of onroad heavy-duty vehicles, beginning in the 2024 model year.

facts.claim: If the resolution fails, California keeps the Environmental Protection Agency's April 6, 2023, permission to enforce four heavy-duty vehicle pollution rules. This affects makers of new heavy-duty vehicles and engines sold in California or in states that have adopted or may adopt California's rules.
facts.quote: This final action will not only affect manufacturers of new heavy-duty vehicles and engines sold in California, but also manufacturers that sell their new heavy-duty vehicles and engines in those states that have already adopted or may choose to adopt California's regulations.

facts.claim: When the Environmental Protection Agency made its April 6, 2023, decision, five other states had adopted California's Advanced Clean Trucks rule on selling zero-emission trucks: Massachusetts, New Jersey, New York, Oregon and Washington.
facts.quote: Massachusetts, New Jersey, New York, Oregon, and Washington have adopted the ACT Regulation.

facts.claim: If the resolution fails, the Environmental Protection Agency's April 6, 2023, decision also lets California require longer emissions warranties for heavy-duty diesel engines and for diesel vehicles over 14,000 pounds powered by them, starting with the 2022 model year.

facts.claim: California's Zero Emission Airport Shuttle rule, one of four covered by the Environmental Protection Agency's April 6, 2023, decision, requires owners of shuttle fleets serving the state's 13 largest airports to have a steadily rising share of zero-emission shuttles.

facts.quote: The ZEP Certification Regulation, adopted by the CARB Board on June 27, 2019, establishes certification requirements and optional emission standards for 2021 and subsequent model year medium- and heavy-duty ZEVs and the zero-emission powertrains installed in such vehicles.

facts.claim: In its April 6, 2023, decision on California's heavy-duty vehicle rules, the Environmental Protection Agency found that California needs its own vehicle pollution program to deal with serious, unusual conditions caused by common air pollutants and, separately, by greenhouse gases.

facts.quote: The term immediate family member, with respect to a foreign person, means the spouse, parent, sibling, or adult child of the person.

facts.claim: Breaking H.R. 23's sanctions would carry the International Emergency Economic Powers Act's penalties. Civil fines can reach $250,000 or twice the deal's value, whichever is greater. Willful violations can bring a fine up to $1,000,000, prison up to 20 years for individuals, or both.
facts.quote: A civil penalty may be imposed on any person who commits an unlawful act described in subsection (a) in an amount not to exceed the greater of— (1) $250,000; or (2) an amount that is twice the amount of the transaction that is the basis of the violation with respect to which the penalty is imposed. (c) Criminal penalty A person who willfully commits, willfully attempts to commit, or willfully conspires to commit, or aids or abets in the commission of, an unlawful act described in subsection (a) shall, upon conviction, be fined not more than $1,000,000, or if a natural person, may be imprisoned for not more than 20 years, or both.

facts.claim: Under H.R. 23, the President may waive the sanctions on a person case by case, for up to 90 days at a time. Before a waiver takes effect, the President must give the relevant committees of Congress a report finding it is essential to U.S. national security interests.
facts.quote: The President may, on a case-by-case basis and for periods not to exceed 90 days each, waive the application of sanctions imposed or maintained with respect to a foreign person under this section if the President submits to the appropriate congressional committees before the waiver is to take effect a report that contains a determination of the President that the waiver is vital to the national security interests of the United States.

facts.claim: Under H.R. 23, the President may end the sanctions if the President certifies in writing to the relevant committees of Congress that the International Criminal Court has stopped every effort to investigate, arrest, detain or prosecute all protected persons, and has permanently closed those efforts.
facts.quote: The President may terminate the sanctions with respect to the foreign persons described in subsection (a) if the President certifies in writing to the appropriate congressional committees that the International Criminal Court— (1)has ceased engaging in any effort to investigate, arrest, detain, or prosecute all protected persons; and(2)has permanently closed, withdrawn, ended, and otherwise terminated any preliminary examination, investigation, or any other effort by the International Criminal Court to investigate, arrest, detain, or prosecute all protected persons.

facts.claim: Under H.R. 23, those protected from the International Criminal Court include every U.S. person, such as current or former U.S. troops and government officials. facts.quote: any United States person, unless the United States provides formal consent to International Criminal Court jurisdiction and is a state party to the Rome Statute of the International Criminal Court, including— (i)current or former members of the Armed Forces of the United States; (ii)current or former elected or appointed officials of the United States Government

facts.claim: In H.R. 23, a "United States person" means a U.S. citizen or permanent resident, a company organized under U.S. law (including its foreign branches), or any person in the United States.
facts.quote: (A)an individual who is a United States citizen or an alien lawfully admitted for permanent residence to the United States; (B)an entity organized under the laws of the United States or any jurisdiction within the United States, including a foreign branch of such an entity; or(C)any person in the United States.

facts.claim: Under H.R. 23, the people protected from the International Criminal Court also include citizens or lawful residents of a U.S. ally that has not accepted the Court's authority or has not joined the Rome Statute, the treaty that set up the Court.
facts.quote: any foreign person that is a citizen or lawful resident of an ally of the United States that has not consented to International Criminal Court jurisdiction or is not a state party to the Rome Statute of the International Criminal Court

facts.claim: In H.R. 23, a U.S. ally means the government of a member country of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO), or of a country designated a "major non-NATO ally" under U.S. law.
facts.quote: (A)a government of a member country of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization; or(B)a government of a major non-NATO ally, as that term is defined by section 2013(7) of the American Service-Members’ Protection Act (22 U.S.C. 7432(7)).

facts.quote: The bipartisan American Servicemembers’ Protection Act was enacted in 2002 to protect United States military personnel, United States officials, and officials and military personnel of certain allied countries against criminal prosecution by an international criminal court to which the United States is not party

facts.claim: H.R. 23's findings note that the United States and Israel are not parties to the Rome Statute (the treaty that set up the International Criminal Court) or members of the Court.
facts.quote: The United States and Israel are not parties to the Rome Statute or members of the International Criminal Court (ICC)

facts.claim: Under current federal law, money provided by any law may not be committed for use by, or support of, the International Criminal Court unless the United States joins the Court by treaty.
facts.quote: None of the funds authorized to be appropriated by this or any other Act may be obligated for use by, or for support of, the International Criminal Court unless the United States has become a party to the Court pursuant to a treaty

facts.claim: Under current federal law, no federal, State or local agency or court may extradite (hand over) anyone from the United States to the International Criminal Court, or give the Court support.

facts.claim: H.R. 6644's limit on large investors buying single-family homes, and its fines, start 180 days after the law was enacted and end 15 years after that start date.

facts.claim: Homes that meet the federal definition of a "manufactured home," which H.R. 6644 changes, are covered by national construction and safety standards. facts.claim: Without H.R. 6644, a "manufactured home" under federal law is a home that is built on a permanent chassis (an undercarriage frame), can be moved in one or more sections, and is designed to be lived in. Such homes are covered by national construction and safety standards.

facts.quote: Any alien who, by fraud or willfully misrepresenting a material fact, seeks to procure (or has sought to procure or has procured) a visa, other documentation, or admission into the United States or other benefit provided under this chapter is inadmissible.

facts.claim: S. 5 uses three grounds to pick out noncitizens who must be held. A third covers an immigrant seeking to enter who lacks a valid visa or other required entry document and a valid passport or other travel document.

facts.claim: S. 5 gives a State's attorney general (its top lawyer) "standing" (the legal right to sue) against the U.S. Attorney General or the Secretary of Homeland Security. The State may sue if a decision to release a noncitizen or to let one out on bond or parole harms the State or its residents.
facts.quote: The attorney general of a State, or other authorized State officer, alleging an action or decision by the Attorney General or Secretary of Homeland Security under this section to release any alien or grant bond or parole to any alien that harms such State or its residents shall have standing to bring an action against the Attorney General or Secretary of Homeland Security

facts.claim: Under S. 5, a State's lawsuit over releasing noncitizens asks a federal district court for a court order (an "injunction"), not money. The court must decide the case as quickly as practical. Harm to a State or its residents includes money losses of more than $100.
facts.quote: in an appropriate district court of the United States to obtain appropriate injunctive relief. The court shall advance on the docket and expedite the disposition of a civil action filed under this subsection to the greatest extent practicable. For purposes of this subsection, a State or its residents shall be considered to have been harmed if the State or its residents experience harm, including financial harm in excess of $100

facts.claim: Immigration law allows parole (temporary permission to enter) only case by case and only for urgent humanitarian reasons or a significant public benefit. S. 5 lets a State's attorney general sue the Secretary of Homeland Security if a breach of that limit harms the State or its residents.
facts.quote: alleging a violation of the limitation under subparagraph (A) that parole solely be granted on a case-by-case basis and solely for urgent humanitarian reasons or a significant public benefit, that harms such State or its residents shall have standing to bring an action against the Secretary of Homeland Security

facts.claim: S. 5 strikes "or release" and "grant" from the current rule that no court may overturn the Attorney General's immigration detention decisions, so decisions to release a noncitizen or to grant bond or parole are no longer shielded from court review.

facts.claim: Without S. 5, immigration law would not add its new group of noncitizens who must be held. facts.quote: On a warrant issued by the Attorney General, an alien may be arrested and detained pending a decision on whether the alien is to be removed from the United States. Except as provided in subsection (c) and pending such decision, the Attorney General— (1) may continue to detain the arrested alien; and (2) may release the alien on— (A) bond of at least $1,500 with security approved by, and containing conditions prescribed by, the Attorney General; or (B) conditional parole

facts.claim: Without S. 5, decisions to release a noncitizen or grant bond or parole would stay shielded from court review. Current immigration law says no court may overturn the Attorney General's decisions to hold or release a noncitizen awaiting a removal decision, or to grant, revoke or deny bond or parole.

facts.claim: Under the Eliminate Shutdowns Act, a program has a "lapse in appropriations" (a gap in its funding) when it was funded in the previous funding law, but neither its full-year funding law for the current budget year nor a temporary ("continuing") funding law is in effect.

facts.claim: Under the Eliminate Shutdowns Act, a program whose funding lapses is automatically provided ("appropriated") money at the same rate as in its most recent funding law, under that law's rules. This applies in every fiscal year (budget year), from its first day.
facts.quote: On and after the first day of each fiscal year, if a lapse in appropriations occurs with respect to a program, project, or activity, there are appropriated such sums as may be necessary, at the rate for operations as provided in the preceding applicable appropriation Acts under the authorities and conditions provided in such Acts

facts.claim: Under the Eliminate Shutdowns Act, the automatic money copies the rate in the latest temporary funding law. If none was enacted this fiscal year, it copies the rate in last year's full-year funding law, not counting extra ("supplemental") funding laws.
facts.quote: the term preceding applicable appropriation Act means—(A)the most recent continuing appropriation Act enacted; or(B)if no continuing appropriation Act has been enacted for the current fiscal year, the most recent applicable full-year appropriation Act (including a full-year continuing appropriation Act) enacted for the immediately preceding fiscal year (excluding any supplemental appropriation Act).

facts.claim: Under the Eliminate Shutdowns Act, a program's automatic money runs from the first day of its funding gap until one of two laws is enacted: a temporary funding law that pays for the program, or a regular funding law for its account (funding heading), even one giving the program nothing.

facts.claim: Executive Order 14257 declared a national emergency over what it called a threat to U.S. security and the economy: unequal tariffs, other trade barriers and trading partners' policies, shown by large, lasting yearly U.S. trade deficits (buying more goods from abroad than the U.S. sells).
facts.quote: find that underlying conditions, including a lack of reciprocity in our bilateral trade relationships, disparate tariff rates and non-tariff barriers, and U.S. trading partners' economic policies that suppress domestic wages and consumption, as indicated by large and persistent annual U.S. goods trade deficits, constitute an unusual and extraordinary threat to the national security and economy of the United States. label: S.Res. 526
title: A resolution withholding the pay of Senators if a Government shutdown occurs.

key_facts.kind: Senate simple resolution (Senators' pay during a lapse in appropriations), adopted
key_facts.about: Drafted with AI from the measure's text and the sources it changes, before the full AI explanation is written. Each fact comes with the exact words that prove it, and a computer checks every quote against the official text. A person has spot-checked 173 of the 513 facts and found none wrong; wording they asked to change has been reworked.

facts.claim: During any government shutdown (a lapse in funding for one or more federal agencies or departments), S.Res. 526 requires the Secretary of the Senate to "disburse and hold" each Senator's pay for that time: set it aside and keep it instead of paying it to the Senator.
facts.quote: During any period in which a Government shutdown is in effect, the Secretary of the Senate shall disburse and hold any payments otherwise required to be made with respect to such period for the compensation of each Senator.

facts.claim: Under S.Res. 526, the Secretary of the Senate must release the pay held from each Senator during a government shutdown as soon as practicable after the shutdown ends: Senators get that pay only after the shutdown, not during it, and do not lose it.
facts.quote: The Secretary of the Senate shall release to each Senator any payments held under paragraph (1) with respect to a Government shutdown as soon as practicable after the date on which the Government shutdown ends.

facts.claim: In S.Res. 526, a government shutdown means a lapse in appropriations (the funding Congress provides by law) for one or more federal agencies or departments. A shutdown of only part of the government counts.
facts.quote: the term Government shutdown means a lapse in appropriations for 1 or more Federal agencies or departments

facts.claim: Under S.Res. 526, the Secretary of the Senate may designate an employee of the Office of the Secretary of the Senate to carry out the holding and release of Senators' pay during government shutdowns.
facts.quote: an employee of the Office of the Secretary of the Senate who is designated by the Secretary to carry out the requirements of this section

facts.claim: If S.Res. 526 is not adopted, the Secretary of the Senate does not hold back Senators' pay during a government shutdown (a lapse in funding for one or more federal agencies). The pay otherwise due for that time is paid as usual, not held until the shutdown ends.
facts.quote: During any period in which a Government shutdown is in effect, the Secretary of the Senate shall disburse and hold any payments otherwise required to be made with respect to such period for the compensation of each Senator.

facts.claim: Under federal law, a federal officer or employee may not spend or commit money beyond what is available in an appropriation (money Congress has provided by law), or commit the government to pay money before Congress provides it, unless a law allows it.
facts.quote: an officer or employee of the United States Government or of the District of Columbia government may not— (A) make or authorize an expenditure or obligation exceeding an amount available in an appropriation or fund for the expenditure or obligation; (B) involve either government in a contract or obligation for the payment of money before an appropriation is made unless authorized by law;

facts.claim: Under federal law, federal employees sent home during a lapse in appropriations (a shutdown) are paid for that time, and those required to keep working are paid for their work. The pay comes at the earliest date possible after the shutdown ends, for shutdowns starting on or after December 22, 2018.
facts.quote: the term "covered lapse in appropriations" means any lapse in appropriations that begins on or after December 22, 2018; (B) the term "District of Columbia public employer" means— (i) the District of Columbia Courts; (ii) the Public Defender Service for the District of Columbia; or (iii) the District of Columbia government; (C) the term "employee" includes an officer; and (D) the term "excepted employee" means an excepted employee or an employee performing emergency work, as such terms are defined by the Office of Personnel Management or the appropriate District of Columbia public employer, as applicable. (2) Each employee of the United States Government or of a District of Columbia public employer furloughed as a result of a covered lapse in appropriations shall be paid for the period of the lapse in appropriations, and each excepted employee who is required to perform work during a covered lapse in appropriations shall be paid for such work, at the employee's standard rate of pay, at the earliest date possible after the lapse in appropriations ends

label: S.Res. 616
title: A resolution requesting information on Honduras's human rights practices pursuant to section 502B(c) of the Foreign Assistance Act of 1961.

key_facts.kind: simple resolution requesting a human rights report under section 502B(c) of the Foreign Assistance Act
key_facts.about: Drafted with AI from the measure's text and the sources it changes, before the full AI explanation is written. Each fact comes with the exact words that prove it, and a computer checks every quote against the official text. A person has spot-checked 173 of the 513 facts and found none wrong; wording they asked to change has been reworked.

facts.claim: S.Res. 616 requests that the Secretary of State send the Senate Foreign Relations and House Foreign Affairs Committees, within 30 days after it is adopted, a statement on Honduras's human rights practices, under section 502B(c) of the Foreign Assistance Act of 1961, a foreign-aid law.
facts.quote: The Senate requests that the Secretary of State, not later than 30 days after the date of the adoption of this resolution, submit to the Committee on Foreign Relations of the Senate and the Committee on Foreign Affairs of the House of Representatives, pursuant to section 502B(c) of the Foreign Assistance Act of 1961

facts.claim: The statement on Honduras that S.Res. 616 requests must include all available credible information on alleged human rights violations by Honduras's government under its former president, including ties between top officials and drug-trafficking groups such as the Sinaloa Cartel.
facts.quote: all available credible information concerning alleged violations of internationally recognized human rights by the Government of the Republic of Honduras under former President Juan Orlando Hernández, including— (A) connections between high-level government officials and drug trafficking organizations, including the Sinaloa Cartel;

facts.claim: The statement on Honduras that S.Res. 616 requests must also cover officials' drug-related corruption, such as money laundering and bribery; torture, rape, illegal detention, witness tampering and murder tied to drug cartels; and efforts to undermine police reforms and drug crime investigations.
facts.quote: (B) corruption of government officials related to drug trafficking, including money laundering and bribery; (C) torture, rape, illegal detention, witness tampering, and murder in connection with drug cartels and drug trafficking; and (D) efforts to undermine police reforms and drug crime investigations;

facts.claim: The statement on Honduras that S.Res. 616 requests must include the Secretary of State's assessment of how likely it is that U.S. security assistance (military and related aid, as federal law defines it) given to Honduras was used to support drug trafficking and related crimes.
facts.quote: an assessment from the Secretary of State of the likelihood that United States security assistance (as defined in section 502B(d) of the Foreign Assistance Act of 1961 ( 22 U.S.C. 2304(d))) provided to the Republic of Honduras has been used in support of activities related to facilitating drug trafficking and its attendant crimes;

facts.claim: The statement on Honduras that S.Res. 616 requests must also describe what the U.S. government has done to promote respect for human rights in the Honduran government's activities and to bring Honduran officials to justice for drug trafficking and related crimes.
facts.quote: (A) to promote respect for and observance of human rights as part of the Government of Honduras’s activities; (B) to bring Honduran government officials to justice for their involvement in drug trafficking and related crimes;

facts.claim: Under section 502B(c) of the Foreign Assistance Act of 1961, if a requested human rights statement on a country is not sent within 30 days of the request, no U.S. security assistance (military and related aid) may go to that country until it is sent, unless a later law specifically allows it.
facts.quote: In the event a statement with respect to a country is requested pursuant to paragraph (1) of this subsection but is not transmitted in accordance therewith within thirty days after receipt of such request, no security assistance shall be delivered to such country except as may thereafter be specifically authorized by law from such country unless and until such statement is transmitted.

facts.claim: If S.Res. 616 is not adopted, the Senate makes no request about Honduras; under section 502B(c) of the Foreign Assistance Act of 1961, the Senate Foreign Relations Committee or the House Foreign Affairs Committee could ask for such a statement on its own, due within 30 days.
facts.quote: or upon the request of the Committee on Foreign Relations of the Senate or the Committee on Foreign Affairs of the House of Representatives, the Secretary of State shall, within thirty days after receipt of such request, transmit to both such committees a statement

facts.claim: Under section 502B(c) of the Foreign Assistance Act of 1961, when the Senate or House by resolution, or either chamber's foreign affairs committee, asks, the Secretary of State must send both committees within 30 days a statement of all available information on human rights in the country named.
facts.quote: Upon the request of the Senate or the House of Representatives by resolution of either such House, or upon the request of the Committee on Foreign Relations of the Senate or the Committee on Foreign Affairs of the House of Representatives, the Secretary of State shall, within thirty days after receipt of such request, transmit to both such committees a statement, prepared with the assistance of the Assistant Secretary of State for Democracy, Human Rights, and Labor, with respect to the country designated in such request, setting forth— (A) all the available information about observance of and respect for human rights and fundamental freedom in that country

facts.claim: The statement on Honduras that S.Res. 616 requests must include the Secretary of State's assessment of the former Honduran president's status since his conviction, and of any ties he still has to drug cartels.
facts.quote: an assessment from the Secretary of State of former President Juan Orlando Hernández’s status post-conviction and any ongoing ties he maintains to drug cartels;

facts.claim: In the human rights section of the Foreign Assistance Act of 1961, "security assistance" includes U.S. military aid, economic support funds, military training, peacekeeping and anti-terrorism aid, and sales of U.S. military equipment and services, with credit and loan guarantees for them.
facts.quote: (A) assistance under part II (military assistance) or part IV (economic support fund) or part V (military education and training) or part VI (peacekeeping operations) or part VIII (antiterrorism assistance) of this subchapter; (B) sales of defense articles or services, extensions of credits (including participations in credits), and guaranties of loans under the Arms Export Control Act

facts.claim: Whether or not S.Res. 616 is adopted, the Foreign Assistance Act of 1961 bars U.S. security assistance to any country whose government engages in a consistent pattern of gross violations of internationally recognized human rights, except in cases that law sets out.
facts.quote: Except under circumstances specified in this section, no security assistance may be provided to any country the government of which engages in a consistent pattern of gross violations of internationally recognized human rights.

facts.claim: Under section 502B(c) of the Foreign Assistance Act of 1961, after the Secretary of State sends a requested human rights statement on a country, Congress may at any time adopt a joint resolution ending, limiting or continuing U.S. security assistance to that country, and the aid must follow it.
facts.quote: In the event a statement with respect to a country is transmitted under paragraph (1) of this subsection, the Congress may at any time thereafter adopt a joint resolution terminating, restricting, or continuing security assistance for such country. In the event such a joint resolution is adopted, such assistance shall be so terminated, so restricted, or so continued, as the case may be.
